questions.q: According to this lesson, what happens to accountability when an organization outsources a function to a vendor?
options: Accountability transfers entirely to the vendor once a contract is signed
Accountability is outsourced, but liability for cost always stays with the original organization
Accountability never transfers — the organization remains responsible to regulators, customers, and its board regardless of which vendor handled the function
Accountability only transfers if the vendor is based in a different country
questions.explain: Outsourcing a function is a reasonable business decision, but accountability for the outcome never leaves the organization — a vendor's failure is still the organization's incident, regulatory exposure, and board conversation.

questions.q: In the widely studied retail breach referenced in this lesson, what was the initial access vector attackers used to get into the retailer's network?
options: Network credentials stolen from a small HVAC and refrigeration contractor with remote monitoring access
A zero-day vulnerability in the retailer's own point-of-sale software
A phishing email sent directly to the retailer's IT administrators
A malicious insider employed directly by the retailer
questions.explain: Attackers used remote-access credentials stolen from an HVAC/refrigeration vendor that had legitimate remote access for monitoring store systems — a vendor relationship that wasn't flagged as high-risk until it became the entry point.

options: Risk introduced by the fourth vendor an organization signs a contract with in a given fiscal year
Risk introduced by a vendor's own subcontractors and suppliers — entities the organization has no direct contract or visibility into
A regulatory classification that only applies to financial services vendors
The risk of a vendor contract expiring without renewal
questions.explain: Fourth-party risk is risk that reaches an organization through its vendor's own vendors — subcontractors and suppliers one layer removed from direct visibility or contractual relationship.

questions.q: Under GDPR, who remains accountable for personal data's protection even when a data processor vendor is the one handling it?
options: The data processor, exclusively, since it physically holds the data
Whichever party's name appears first in the data processing agreement
No one, until a regulator formally assigns blame after an investigation
The data controller — the organization that determines why and how the data is processed
questions.explain: GDPR draws a clear line: the data controller decides why and how personal data is processed and remains accountable for its protection, even when a processor vendor handles the data on its behalf.

questions.q: What do the three breach patterns described in this lesson — stolen vendor credentials, a poisoned software update, and mass exploitation of one shared product — have in common?
options: All three required the victim organization to have clicked a phishing link first
All three only affected government agencies, never private enterprises
In each case, the victims' own security controls weren't the weak point — a vendor relationship was
All three were caused by the same group of attackers using the same technique
questions.explain: Despite different mechanisms (stolen credentials, a compromised update process, mass exploitation of a shared product), each pattern shares the same underlying lesson: the entry point was a vendor relationship, not a direct failure in the victim's own controls.
